# Tree-based structures (Octree, Pointer Tree, Sparse Voxel DAG)

Also called: Sparse Voxel Trees, Hierarchical Voxel Grids, Subdivision Trees

## Overview
Tree-based structures represent volumetric data using a recursive spatial subdivision where empty or uniform regions are collapsed into single nodes, providing [compression](#4-compression.md) proportional to data sparsity [G]. This family solves the memory and bandwidth bottlenecks of dense [voxel grids](#1719-voxel-grid-indexing.md) by enabling efficient culling of empty space and adaptive resolution [G]. Unlike sibling structures like [Hash Grids](#936-hash-grids.md) or [Brick Maps](#2793-brick-based-hierarchical-storage.md) which rely on flat hashing or fixed-size blocks, tree-based methods prioritize [hierarchical traversal](#896-hierarchical-traversal.md) and spatial locality, allowing for variable depth and explicit parent-child relationships that facilitate complex operations like neighbor lookups and level-of-detail (LOD) generation [G].

## Shared principles
All structures in this family share the following mechanism:

1.  **[Recursive Subdivision](#1304-recursive-subdivision.md):** The 3D domain is recursively divided into sub-volumes. In standard octrees, each node has 8 children. In pointer trees, the branching factor $N$ varies ($N^3$ children).
2.  **Sparsity Encoding:** Empty regions are represented by null pointers or absence of children, rather than storing zero-valued voxels. This provides compression proportional to the sparsity of the data.
3.  **Hierarchical Traversal:** Rendering or access requires traversing from the root to the leaf. This allows skipping large empty volumes (culling) and adapting resolution to view distance or detail requirements.
4.  **Spatial Locality:** Children of a node are spatially contiguous. This locality is often exploited via Morton ordering (Z-order curve) to map 3D coordinates to 1D keys, enabling efficient neighbor lookups and linear array representations in implicit variants [G].
5.  **Subtree Merging:** The core differentiator of the DAG family is the identification of structurally identical subtrees (isomorphic nodes) and their replacement with a single shared instance. This transforms the tree topology into a graph where multiple parents may reference the same child node, eliminating redundancy [S1][S2].

## Subtopics

### [Compact pointer tree](844-compact-pointer-tree.md)
Uses variable branching factor $N$ ($2 \le N \le 6$) and compact 8-bit relative pointers to optimize memory for terabyte-scale [RGBA](#5142-color-packing-rgba.md) data on GPUs. It combines wavelet-based color compression with [hierarchical DDA](#5710-hierarchical-dda.md) traversal.

### [Sparse Voxel DAGs](2791-sparse-voxel-dags.md)
Merges identical subtrees into shared nodes to reduce memory footprint by 1-3 orders of magnitude compared to standard trees. It decouples geometric hierarchy from material attributes and employs bottom-up reduction or hash-based recycling.

### [Octree-based structures](2792-octree-based-structures.md)
Relies on a fixed 8-way branching factor and explicit or implicit parent-child pointers. It prioritizes hierarchical traversal and spatial locality over the deduplication or pointer-free compactness of DAGs or variable-branching trees.

### [Span Space Tree](4379-span-space-tree.md)
Organizes data along axis-aligned spans (intervals) rather than just voxel occupancy. It refines the interval tree concept to manage scene complexity, allowing for more efficient culling of empty or uniform regions during [ray casting](#6080-ray-casting.md).

### [Sparse Voxel Tree (SVO Tree)](4983-sparse-voxel-tree-svo-tree.md)
A standard hierarchical structure with a fixed branching factor of 8. It allocates memory only for non-empty regions, providing compression proportional to sparsity, but allows multiple paths to the same voxel (no sharing).

### [Tiny LOD](6968-tiny-lod.md)
Constructs a hierarchical LOD tree from splat data, parameterized by a base LOD value and a merge filter flag. It outputs encoded opacity values and a [chunk tree](#4050-chunk-trees.md), distinguished by its specific procedural pipeline for splat-based rendering.

### [NerfTree](7559-nerftree.md)
A two-level [octree structure](#2792-octree-based-structures.md) for [Neural Radiance Fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) ([NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md)). It uses a coarse density volume to cache approximate geometry and fine [sparse voxel grids](#8430-sparse-spatial-data-structures-for-nerf.md) for refinement, reducing MLP evaluations by skipping empty space.

### [Adaptively Sampled Distance Fields](7773-adaptively-sampled-distance-fields.md)
Compresses [Signed Distance Fields](#1466-signed-distance-fields-sdf.md) (SDFs) by exploiting smoothness. It uses adaptive simplification with a strict sign-preservation constraint to maintain topological accuracy of the zero isosurface, enabling resolution-independent [antialiasing](#4802-antialiasing-aa.md).

## Background
Tree-based structures originated in the 1980s as a solution to the "curse of dimensionality" in spatial data indexing, with octrees being one of the earliest forms [G]. In computer graphics, they were adopted in the 1990s for [ray tracing and volume rendering](#2419-volume-ray-casting-with-barycentric-interpolation-and-phong-.md) to handle sparse scenes efficiently [G]. The [Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO)](#8749-sparse-voxel-octree-svo.md) became a standard for high-quality volume rendering in the 2000s, enabling interactive frame rates for large datasets [G]. Recent developments include DAGs for deduplication [S1][S2], [compact pointer trees](#844-compact-pointer-tree.md) for GPU efficiency [S1][S2], and adaptations for NeRF [S1] and SDFs [S1].
